[SYSTEM]
You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: The query is itraconazole; L6 C225 directly names itraconazole as hepatically metabolized and a CYP substrate/inhibitor, providing mechanistic presystemic-loss evidence, but no L6 card reports an F<20% outcome for itraconazole.

L4 shows close analogs posaconazole and ketoconazole are highly Caco-2 permeable (posaconazole Papp ~3.4-4.0×10^-5 cm/s; ketoconazole high passive permeability), supporting intestinal absorption for the lipophilic azole scaffold.

L3 oral exposure records for posaconazole show substantial systemic exposure after oral dosing (AUC 8619 ng·h/mL, Cmax 851 ng/mL at 400 mg BID suspension), and L1 contexts with measured F ≥49% (apixaban 49%, ziprasidone ~60%, vilazodone 72%, delpazolid 99.75%, MMV367 90%) support F≥20% as a transferable endpoint calibration.

L6 posaconazole records show low hepatic first-pass loss (Fh 0.94, minimal CYP metabolism, ~17% UGT), but C225 distinguishes itraconazole as hepatically metabolized, so posaconazole hepatic-transfer is limited.

L5 C212 directly identifies itraconazole as a P-gp substrate, and L6 ketoconazole analog records show CYP3A4-mediated metabolism and moderate-to-high hepatic extraction in some rat studies; these are presystemic-loss caveats but not affirmative threshold-relevant evidence for F<20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for itraconazole is present in the supplied cards; prediction remains transfer-based.
No fasted-state-specific F, solubility, or dissolution data for the query itself; L4/L6 values are for close analogs and mostly buffer/FaSSIF/duodenal media or non-query species.
L6 hepatic-clearance records are mostly for ketoconazole/posaconazole; only C225 directly names itraconazole and is qualitative.
No quantitative link between P-gp/CYP3A4-mediated presystemic loss and F<20% is established for itraconazole.
Conflicting hepatic extraction estimates for ketoconazole (HER 0.6 vs Eh 5%) limit quantitative transfer.
Structural differences between query and M01/M02 (triazolone vs imidazole/acetyl-piperazine, sec-butyl triazole side chain) may affect transferability.
content.decision_summary: Predicted high (F >= 20%) remains supported: L4 shows close analogs posaconazole and ketoconazole are highly Caco-2 permeable, L3/L1 provide substantial oral exposure and transferable measured F values >=49%, and L6 posaconazole records show low hepatic first-pass loss. L6 adds direct mechanistic evidence that itraconazole is hepatically metabolized (C225) and ketoconazole analog metabolism/efflux records, which are presystemic-loss caveats but not affirmative threshold-relevant evidence for F<20%. Confidence remains moderate because the evidence is transfer-based and lacks a direct fasted itraconazole F measurement.

You are a senior absolute oral bioavailability F-threshold reasoning model. Integrate evidence direction and transferability without converting uncertainty into a negative outcome. 

L6 adds hepatic-clearance and metabolic-stability experiments. Use them as mechanistic evidence for systemic presystemic loss while preserving species, assay system, and measurement direction; they are not direct oral- bioavailability results or extra gold votes.

This is progressive assay-transfer reasoning. The target is the task endpoint,
not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.
